title: Hafsah, keeper of pages
hook: Umar's daughter, in whose house the gathered sheets of the Qur'an were kept (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aisha, who checked what she heard against the text. Your line was: she taught the teachers. Did your question find someone to answer it? Day eight hundred ten.

A messenger knocks at a woman's door with a request from the caliph Uthman. Please send us the sheets, so we can copy them. We will return them to you. What she has in her house is not jewelry and not a treasury. It is a set of written pages, gathered by careful hands, that she has been trusted to keep. The whole community is about to depend on them. Today: Hafsah.
screen: `A KNOCK FROM THE CALIPH.` → `SEND US THE SHEETS.` → `WE WILL RETURN THEM.`

segments.voice: Hafsah was the daughter of Umar ibn al-Khattab and a wife of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Her place in this story comes from two reports in Sahih al-Bukhari, told one after the other. The first is a gathering. After a battle in which many who knew the Qur'an by heart were killed, Umar urged Abu Bakr to collect the Qur'an in writing. Abu Bakr hesitated: how could he do something the Prophet had not done? In the end he agreed, and gave the task to Zayd ibn Thabit. Zayd says it would have been easier to move a mountain. He searched for the verses, gathering them from what was written and from the memories of men. The sheets, Bukhari says, stayed with Abu Bakr until he died, then with Umar for the rest of his life, and then with Hafsah, daughter of Umar. The second report is the knock at her door. In Uthman's time, people in distant lands were reciting differently and arguing over it. Uthman sent to Hafsah, asking for the sheets so they could be copied, with a promise to return them. She sent them. Copies were made and sent out to the regions. And the sheets went back to Hafsah. Look at what kind of honor this is. Hafsah did not write the pages or gather them. She kept them. When the community needed a trusted standard, it knew exactly whose house to ask, and the pages came back to the place they had been safe. Keeping is quiet work, and it is real work. She kept the pages.
screen: `ZAYD GATHERS THE VERSES.` · `ABU BAKR, THEN UMAR, THEN HAFSAH.` · `UTHMAN SENDS TO HER DOOR.` · `THE SHEETS COME BACK TO HER.` · then, large: `SHE KEPT THE PAGES.`

segments.voice: The practice: keep something precious safe. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've been trusted with. A letter, a photograph, a recipe, a secret someone told you, a copy of a holy book on your shelf. Picture where it is right now. Is it safe there? Would it come back to you if you lent it? Breathe in, and hold it in mind with care. If you pray, you can give thanks for what has been placed in your keeping. The bell holds the time.
Hafsah. Umar's daughter and a mother of the believers, in whose house the gathered sheets of the Qur'an were kept, lent for copying, and returned. Today's word.
Your line: she kept the pages. Today, put one precious thing somewhere safe, or give back something you've borrowed. Day eight hundred ten.

howItsDone: Muslims who study how the Qur'an was gathered learn the reports in Sahih al-Bukhari of Zayd ibn Thabit's collection under Abu Bakr and Uthman's copying from the sheets kept by Hafsah.

fork.setup: you are Hafsah. the caliph asks for the sheets in your keeping, to make copies for distant lands. what do you do?
options: refuse, because they were trusted to you.
send them, on his promise to return them.
copy them yourself and keep the originals.
fork.reveal: Bukhari says she sent them, copies were made and sent out, and the sheets were returned to her.

original.note: Arabic: 'sheets', the word for the pages kept with Hafsah.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hafsah was simply Umar's daughter.
what it means: she was trusted to keep the gathered sheets of the Qur'an, and lent them for the copies.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 4986 for Zayd's gathering and the sheets passing to Hafsah; Bukhari 4987 for Uthman's copying and their return.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4986 (Zayd ibn Thabit collects the Qur'an under Abu Bakr; the sheets pass to Umar, then Hafsah)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 (Uthman asks Hafsah for the sheets, copies them, returns them)
